claim: Drosophila larvae navigate by initiating turns in response to temporally varying sensory input.
source: To better understand how organisms make decisions on the basis of temporally varying multi-sensory input, we identified computations made by Drosophila larvae responding to visual and optogenetically induced fictive olfactory stimuli.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as the basis for the study.

claim: The larva's navigational decision to initiate turns can be modeled as the output of a Linear-Nonlinear-Poisson cascade.
source: We modeled the larva's navigational decision to initiate turns as the output of a Linear-Nonlinear-Poisson cascade.
evidence: This is the core modeling approach described in the abstract and methods.

claim: Reverse-correlation can be used to fit parameters to the LNP model for larval navigation.
source: We used reverse-correlation to fit parameters to this model; the parameterized model predicted larvae's responses to novel stimulus patterns.
evidence: The abstract states this method was used and validated.

claim: Larvae linearly combine olfactory and visual signals upstream of the decision to turn.
source: For multi-modal inputs, we found that larvae linearly combine olfactory and visual signals upstream of the decision to turn.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Larvae integrate odor and light according to the same rule for all navigational decisions.
source: We studied other navigational decisions and found that larvae integrated odor and light according to the same rule in all cases.
evidence: This is stated as a finding in the abstract.

claim: Photo-taxis and odor-taxis are mediated by a shared computational pathway.
source: These results suggest that photo-taxis and odor-taxis are mediated by a shared computational pathway.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract.

claim: Many small organisms navigate by decoding temporal variations in receptor activity to bias motor output decisions.
source: Many small organisms navigate their environments by decoding temporal variations in receptor activity to bias motor output decisions (Berg and Brown, 1972; Sawin et al., 1994; Pierce-Shimomura et al., 1999; Ryu and Samuel, 2002; Fishilevich et al., 2005; Louis et al., 2008; Luo et al., 2008, 2010; Albrecht and Bargmann, 2011; Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Lockery, 2011; Gershow et al., 2012; Kane et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations in the introduction.

claim: The dynamics of organisms' decision-making are linked to properties of underlying chemical or neural substrates.
source: The dynamics of these organisms' decision-making are intimately linked to the properties of the underlying chemical or neural substrates (Segall et al., 1986; Korobkova et al., 2004; Miller et al., 2005; Chronis et al., 2007; Clark et al., 2007; Emonet and Cluzel, 2008; Suzuki et al., 2008; Asahina et al., 2009; Shimizu et al., 2010; Bretscher et al., 2011; Busch et al., 2012; Kato et al., 2014; Luo et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Second instar Drosophila larvae use a similar strategy for navigating environments with spatially varying odor concentrations, light levels, and temperatures.
source: The second instar larva uses a similar strategy for navigating environments with spatially varying odor concentrations, light levels, and temperatures.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations.

claim: Larvae move forward in a series of relatively straight runs interspersed with reorienting turns.
source: Larvae move forward in a series of relatively straight runs interspersed with reorienting turns, and increase the frequency and magnitude of their turns in response to unfavorable changes in the stimulus (Sawin et al., 1994; Busto et al., 1999; Scantlebury et al., 2007; Louis et al., 2008; Luo et al., 2010; Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gershow et al., 2012; Kane et al., 2013; Klein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a well-established behavioral pattern supported by multiple citations.

claim: Larvae increase the frequency and magnitude of their turns in response to unfavorable changes in the stimulus.
source: Larvae move forward in a series of relatively straight runs interspersed with reorienting turns, and increase the frequency and magnitude of their turns in response to unfavorable changes in the stimulus (Sawin et al., 1994; Busto et al., 1999; Scantlebury et al., 2007; Louis et al., 2008; Luo et al., 2010; Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gershow et al., 2012; Kane et al., 2013; Klein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: During turns, larvae survey the local environment using side-to-side head sweeps to determine the direction of the next run.
source: During turns, larvae survey the local environment using side-to-side head sweeps to determine the direction of the next run (Sawin et al., 1994; Luo et al., 2010; Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gershow et al., 2012; Kane et al., 2013; Klein et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The Linear-Nonlinear-Poisson (LNP) model is widely used to relate time-varying input to stochastic output.
source: The Linear-Nonlinear-Poisson (LNP) model (Chichilnisky, 2001; Dayan, 2001; Ringach and Shapley, 2004; Bialek and van Steveninck, 2005; Schwartz et al., 2006; Kim et al., 2011) is widely used to relate time-varying input to stochastic output.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: In the LNP model, decisions are generated according to a Poisson process whose underlying rate at time t is r(t)=f[(A∗S)(t)].
source: In this model, decisions (e.g., to initiate a turn, Figure 1A,B) are generated according to a Poisson process whose underlying rate at time t is:r(t)=f[(A∗S)(t)];(A∗S)(t)=∫0∞A(τ)S(t−τ)dτ,where S(t) is the input signal, A is a linear filter, and f is a static nonlinear function (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is the mathematical definition of the LNP model used in the study, shown in text and Figure 1B.

claim: Drosophila larvae avoid light and carbon dioxide.
source: Drosophila larvae avoid light and carbon dioxide and are attracted to Ethyl Acetate (EtAc).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Results section.

claim: Drosophila larvae are attracted to Ethyl Acetate (EtAc).
source: Drosophila larvae avoid light and carbon dioxide and are attracted to Ethyl Acetate (EtAc).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Results section.

claim: The larva's navigational response to light is mediated primarily by four photoreceptor neurons in each of two primitive eye-spots.
source: The larva's navigational response to light is mediated primarily by four photoreceptor neurons in each of two primitive eye-spots (Hassan et al., 2005; Sprecher and Desplan, 2008; Keene et al., 2011; Keene and Sprecher, 2012; Kane et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A single pair of Gr21a expressing receptor neurons mediates the larva's CO2 response.
source: A single pair of Gr21a expressing receptor neurons mediates the larva's CO2 response (Python and Stocker, 2002; Faucher, 2006; Jones et al., 2007; Kwon et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Or42a and Or42b are the primary EtAc olfactory receptors.
source: Or42a and Or42b are the primary EtAc olfactory receptors (Kreher et al., 2005, 2008; Asahina et al., 2009), and larvae are capable of decoding odor gradients on the basis of only Or42a or Or42b receptor neurons (Louis et al., 2008; Asahina et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Larvae are capable of decoding odor gradients on the basis of only Or42a or Or42b receptor neurons.
source: Or42a and Or42b are the primary EtAc olfactory receptors (Kreher et al., 2005, 2008; Asahina et al., 2009), and larvae are capable of decoding odor gradients on the basis of only Or42a or Or42b receptor neurons (Louis et al., 2008; Asahina et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Larvae initiate turns in response to increasing light intensities.
source: Larvae initiate turns in response to increasing light intensities (Sawin et al., 1994; Hassan et al., 2005; Scantlebury et al., 2007; Kane et al., 2013) and carbon dioxide concentrations (Gershow et al., 2012) and decreasing EtAc concentrations (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gershow et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Larvae initiate turns in response to increasing carbon dioxide concentrations.
source: Larvae initiate turns in response to increasing light intensities (Sawin et al., 1994; Hassan et al., 2005; Scantlebury et al., 2007; Kane et al., 2013) and carbon dioxide concentrations (Gershow et al., 2012) and decreasing EtAc concentrations (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gershow et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Larvae initiate turns in response to decreasing EtAc concentrations.
source: Larvae initiate turns in response to increasing light intensities (Sawin et al., 1994; Hassan et al., 2005; Scantlebury et al., 2007; Kane et al., 2013) and carbon dioxide concentrations (Gershow et al., 2012) and decreasing EtAc concentrations (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gershow et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: CsChrimson is a red light activable cation channel.
source: To probe olfactory computations, we expressed UAS-CsChrimson (Klapoetke et al., 2014), a red light activable cation channel, in Gr21a, Or42a, and Or42b receptor neuron pairs.
evidence: This is stated in the methods and supported by citation.

claim: 655 nm red light is outside the sensitive range of the larva's visual pigments.
source: We used 655 nm red light (outside the sensitive range of the larva's visual pigments [Salcedo et al., 1999]) to activate these neurons while presenting a constant dim blue light background (Klapoetke et al., 2014) to mask any visual response to the red light.
evidence: This is stated and supported by citation.

claim: For light, odor, and carbon dioxide, the derivative of stimulus intensity is more salient to larvae than the stimulus value itself.
source: For light, odor, and carbon dioxide, the derivative of stimulus intensity is more salient to larvae than the stimulus value itself (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gershow et al., 2012; Kane et al., 2013; Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Wild-type larvae turn in response to an increase in blue light.
source: We found: wild-type larvae turn in response to an increase in blue light but were unresponsive to red light masked by dim blue light (even when fed all-trans-retinal)
evidence: This is a finding from the reverse-correlation experiments described in the Results.

claim: Wild-type larvae are unresponsive to red light masked by dim blue light.
source: We found: wild-type larvae turn in response to an increase in blue light but were unresponsive to red light masked by dim blue light (even when fed all-trans-retinal)
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments.

claim: Larvae expressing CsChrimson in EtAc sensing neurons (Or42a>CsChrimson, Or42b>CsChrimson) turned in response to a decrease in red light.
source: larvae expressing CsChrimson in EtAc sensing neurons (Or42a>CsChrimson, Or42b>CsChrimson) turned in response to a decrease in red light
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments.

claim: Larvae expressing CsChrimson in the CO2 receptor (Gr21a>CsChrimson) turned in response to an increase in red light.
source: larvae expressing CsChrimson in the CO2 receptor (Gr21a>CsChrimson) turned in response to an increase in red light.
evidence: This is a finding from the experiments.

claim: Larvae considered changes over the previous ~2.5 s when deciding to turn.
source: In all cases (excepting the wild-type red-light control), larvae considered changes over the previous ∼2.5 s when deciding to turn, and derivatives were maximally salient about 0.6–0.8 s before a turn was actually initiated.
evidence: This is inferred from the turn-triggered average analysis.

claim: Derivatives were maximally salient about 0.6–0.8 s before a turn was actually initiated.
source: In all cases (excepting the wild-type red-light control), larvae considered changes over the previous ∼2.5 s when deciding to turn, and derivatives were maximally salient about 0.6–0.8 s before a turn was actually initiated.
evidence: This is inferred from the turn-triggered average analysis.

claim: The LNP model predicted the temporal course of the larva's response to step changes surprisingly well.
source: We found that in all cases, except for Gr21a>CsChrimson, the step response has a longer duration than predicted by the LNP model, and there is an unpredicted sustained decrease in turn rate following a favorable change (at t = 0), but given the inherent variability of behavior and the simplicity of the LNP model, the reverse-correlation experiments predicted the temporal course of the larva's response to step changes surprisingly well.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing model predictions to experimental data in Figure 2C.

claim: For visual and attractive odor inputs, larvae were slightly less responsive to stimulus changes in the latter half of the experiments.
source: We found that for visual and attractive odor inputs, the slope of the nonlinear function was steeper (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) in the first 10 min than in the second 10, indicating larvae were slightly less responsive to stimulus changes in the latter half of the experiments.
evidence: This is inferred from analysis of data split by time, shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: For fictive CO2, larvae were more responsive in the second 10 min, representing sensitization rather than adaptation.
source: For fictive CO2, on the other hand, we found that larvae were actually more responsive in the second 10 min, representing sensitization rather than adaptation.
evidence: This is inferred from analysis of data split by time.

claim: Larvae make larger turns when subjected to unfavorably changing conditions.
source: Larvae make larger turns when subjected to unfavorably changing conditions (Luo et al., 2010; Gershow et al., 2012; Kane et al., 2013), so we calculated the TTA for large and small turns separately (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by citations and analyzed in Figure 2D.

claim: For approximately 10–15 s prior to the start of large turns, there was an average gradual increase in blue light levels for visual experiments.
source: For approximately 10–15 s prior to the start of large turns, there was an average gradual increase in blue light levels for visual experiments, and an average gradual decrease in red light levels for Or42a>CsChrimson and Or42b>CsChrimson experiments.
evidence: This is observed in the size-sorted TTA analysis.

claim: Immediately prior to the initiation of a turn, the average change in stimulus was the same for large and small turns.
source: Interestingly, immediately prior to the initiation of a turn, the average change in stimulus was the same for large and small turns.
evidence: This is observed in the size-sorted TTA analysis.

claim: Larvae consider the change in light intensity and attractive odor concentration over the previous 10–15 s when deciding the size of their turns.
source: Thus, larvae consider the change in light intensity and attractive odor concentration over the previous 10–15 s when deciding the size of their turns, but the size of the stimulus change that leads the larva to actually initiate a turn appears not to influence turn size.
evidence: This is inferred from the size-sorted TTA analysis.

claim: The size of the stimulus change that leads the larva to actually initiate a turn appears not to influence turn size for light and attractive odor.
source: Thus, larvae consider the change in light intensity and attractive odor concentration over the previous 10–15 s when deciding the size of their turns, but the size of the stimulus change that leads the larva to actually initiate a turn appears not to influence turn size.
evidence: This is inferred from the size-sorted TTA analysis.

claim: For Gr21a>CsChrimson larvae, the size of a turn was determined by the magnitude of the increase immediately preceding a turn.
source: In contrast, for Gr21a>CsChrimson larvae, the size of a turn was determined by the magnitude of the increase immediately preceding a turn.
evidence: This is observed in the size-sorted TTA analysis for CO2.

claim: Head-sweeps in favorable directions are more likely to be accepted, beginning a new run in that direction.
source: Head-sweeps in favorable directions are more likely to be accepted, beginning a new run in that direction. Head-sweeps in unfavorable directions are more likely to be rejected, resulting in one or more additional head-sweeps.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: Head-sweeps in unfavorable directions are more likely to be rejected, resulting in one or more additional head-sweeps.
source: Head-sweeps in favorable directions are more likely to be accepted, beginning a new run in that direction. Head-sweeps in unfavorable directions are more likely to be rejected, resulting in one or more additional head-sweeps.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: During accepted head-sweeps, average blue light levels and Gr21a activity decreased and Or42a and Or42b activity increased.
source: We found that during accepted head-sweeps, average blue light levels and Gr21a activity decreased and Or42a and Or42b activity increased, all favorable changes.
evidence: This is observed in the head-sweep triggered average analysis.

claim: During rejected head-sweeps, average blue light and Gr21a activity levels increased and Or42a and Or42b activity decreased.
source: During rejected head-sweeps, the reverse was true: average blue light and Gr21a activity levels increased and Or42a and Or42b activity decreased.
evidence: This is observed in the head-sweep triggered average analysis.

claim: For Gr21a>CsChrimson larvae, larger increases in activity prior to the head-sweep start led to an increased probability of rejecting the head-sweep.
source: Surprisingly, for Gr21a>CsChrimson larvae, larger increases in activity prior to the head-sweep start led to an increased probability of rejecting the head-sweep.
evidence: This is observed in the head-sweep triggered average analysis.

claim: CsChrimson induced activity in olfactory neurons evokes navigational behaviors.
source: Our uni-modal experiments showed that CsChrimson induced activity in olfactory neurons evokes navigational behaviors and that reverse correlation can be used to identify both visual and olfactory computations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the uni-modal experiments.

claim: Reverse correlation can be used to identify both visual and olfactory computations.
source: Our uni-modal experiments showed that CsChrimson induced activity in olfactory neurons evokes navigational behaviors and that reverse correlation can be used to identify both visual and olfactory computations.
evidence: This is a conclusion from the uni-modal experiments.

claim: Activity in CO2 receptor neurons is interpreted according to different rules than for light or attractive odors.
source: We also found that activity in CO2 receptor neurons is interpreted according to different rules than for light or attractive odors.
evidence: This is a conclusion from comparing the different behavioral responses.

claim: In the independent pathways model, the mixed partial derivative of turn rate with respect to odor and light filter outputs is identically 0.
source: In general, this value will be nonzero, but in the independent pathways model (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), the mixed partial derivative is identically 0
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the independent pathways model.

claim: The early linear combination model better predicted the turn-triggered probability density than the independent pathways model.
source: We used both the independent pathways and early linear combination models to fit the turn-triggered probability density of (xO, xL) and found better agreement between the data and the early linear combination prediction (Figure 3D) than the independent pathways prediction (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a conclusion from model comparison shown in Figures 3C and 3D.

claim: The parameter u alone is nearly as informative as both xO and xL together about the decision to turn.
source: we calculated this divergence for the pair (xO, xL) and for xO, xL, u, and v individually (Figure 3B) and found that u alone is nearly as informative as both xO and xL and that v contributes very little to the decision to turn, further supporting the early linear combination model.
evidence: This is calculated from Kullback-Leibler divergence analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The parameter v contributes very little to the decision to turn.
source: we calculated this divergence for the pair (xO, xL) and for xO, xL, u, and v individually (Figure 3B) and found that u alone is nearly as informative as both xO and xL and that v contributes very little to the decision to turn, further supporting the early linear combination model.
evidence: This is calculated from Kullback-Leibler divergence analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Blind larvae expressing CsChrimson in Or42a neurons responded only to red light.
source: Blind larvae responded only to red light (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B) while larvae not expressing CsChrimson responded only to blue light (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Larvae not expressing CsChrimson responded only to blue light.
source: Blind larvae responded only to red light (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B) while larvae not expressing CsChrimson responded only to blue light (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The early linear combination model better predicted the response to conflicting and aligned multi-sensory input than the independent pathways model.
source: We found that despite having fewer free fit parameters, the early linear combination model (magenta line, Figure 4) better predicted the response to conflicting and aligned multi-sensory input than the independent pathways model (cyan line, Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 comparing model predictions to data.

claim: For changes in only light or only odor, larvae increase their turn rates significantly more for unfavorable changes than they decrease their turning in response to favorable changes.
source: For changes in only light or only odor, larvae increase their turn rates significantly more for unfavorable changes (panels ii and iii) than they decrease their turning in response to favorable changes (i and vi).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 4.

claim: Conflicting changes in odor and light cancel each other out.
source: Instead, conflicting changes in odor and light cancel each other out, as predicted by the early linear combination model.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 4 for conflicting stimuli.

claim: Larvae turn in response to increases in blue light but decreases in red light, confirming that the two light sources are activating different sensory pathways.
source: That larvae turn in response to increases in blue light (iii, v) but decreases in red light (ii, v) further confirms that the two light sources are activating different sensory pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential responses to blue and red light in Figure 4.

claim: The turn triggered average of ν(t) was nearly 0.
source: We found: the turn triggered average of ν(t) was nearly 0 (Figure 5A); the size-sorted TTA of ν(t) was nearly 0 and the same for both small and large turns (Figure 5B); and the head-sweep triggered average of ν(t) was nearly 0 and the same for accepted and rejected head-sweeps (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The size-sorted TTA of ν(t) was nearly 0 and the same for both small and large turns.
source: We found: the turn triggered average of ν(t) was nearly 0 (Figure 5A); the size-sorted TTA of ν(t) was nearly 0 and the same for both small and large turns (Figure 5B); and the head-sweep triggered average of ν(t) was nearly 0 and the same for accepted and rejected head-sweeps (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The head-sweep triggered average of ν(t) was nearly 0 and the same for accepted and rejected head-sweeps.
source: We found: the turn triggered average of ν(t) was nearly 0 (Figure 5A); the size-sorted TTA of ν(t) was nearly 0 and the same for both small and large turns (Figure 5B); and the head-sweep triggered average of ν(t) was nearly 0 and the same for accepted and rejected head-sweeps (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Larvae used a single linear combination of odor and light—μ(t)—to determine whether to turn, how large of a turn to make, and whether to reject or accept head-sweeps.
source: Thus, larvae used a single linear combination of odor and light—μ(t)—to determine whether to turn, how large of a turn to make, and whether to reject or accept head-sweeps, strongly suggesting odor and light inputs are combined at early stages of the navigational circuitry.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis in Figure 5.

claim: Odor and light inputs are combined at early stages of the navigational circuitry.
source: Thus, larvae used a single linear combination of odor and light—μ(t)—to determine whether to turn, how large of a turn to make, and whether to reject or accept head-sweeps, strongly suggesting odor and light inputs are combined at early stages of the navigational circuitry.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that a single linear combination is used for all decisions.

claim: Regardless of which stimulus likely triggered the decision to turn, for both light and odor, the same differences between accepted and rejected head-sweeps were found.
source: Regardless of which stimulus likely triggered the decision to turn, for both light and odor, we found the same differences between accepted and rejected head-sweeps.
evidence: This is observed in Figure 6B.

claim: There is no evidence that the larva modulated the relative importance of light or odor changes when deciding whether to accept or reject a head-sweep.
source: Thus, we found no evidence that the larva modulated the relative importance of light or odor changes when deciding whether to accept or reject a head-sweep.
evidence: This is concluded from the analysis in Figure 6.

claim: For all combinations of light and odor changes preceding a turn, the same linear combination of odor and light inputs appeared to be equally salient in deciding whether to accept or reject a head-sweep.
source: Indeed, for all combinations of light and odor changes preceding a turn, the same linear combination of odor and light inputs appeared to be equally salient in deciding whether to accept or reject a head-sweep (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Reverse-correlation analysis captured the essential features of the larva's navigational decision making, including the time scales and stimulus features associated with various decisions.
source: Here, we carried on this refinement, quantifying the transformation from sensory activity to motor decision with sub-second temporal resolution. Our reverse-correlation analysis captured the essential features of the larva's navigational decision making, including the time scales and stimulus features associated with various decisions (Figure 2).
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion in the Discussion and supported by Figure 2.

claim: Larvae mainly use only the previous two seconds of receptor activity to decide whether to turn.
source: Additionally, we showed that larvae mainly use only the previous two seconds of receptor activity to decide whether to turn (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is inferred from the TTA analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Larvae integrate changes in odor receptor activity over a much longer time period to decide the size of their turns.
source: This detail cannot be resolved from experiments in natural odor gradients, nor can the fact that larvae integrate changes in odor receptor activity over a much longer time period to decide the size of their turns (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is inferred from the size-sorted TTA analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Warming a cold larva during a head-sweep causes the larva to accept that head-sweep, beginning a new run.
source: It has been directly shown that warming a cold larva during a head-sweep causes the larva to accept that head-sweep, beginning a new run (Luo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Larvae are more likely to begin a run following a sweep in a direction of higher concentration of attractive odor, lower concentration of carbon dioxide, or lower luminosity.
source: For light and odor, a strong circumstantial case has been made that larvae use information gathered during head-sweeps to bias turn direction: the first head-sweep of a turn is unbiased (Gershow et al., 2012; Kane et al., 2013) but larvae are more likely to begin a run following a sweep in a direction of higher concentration of attractive odor, lower concentration of carbon dioxide, or lower luminosity (Gomez-Marin et al., 2011; Gershow et al., 2012; Kane et al., 2013; Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2014)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Larvae with only a single functional odor receptor can still bias turn direction via head-sweeping.
source: and larvae with only a single functional odor receptor can still bias turn direction via head-sweeping (Gomez-Marin and Louis, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: Larvae do in fact use changes in odor receptor activity and light level measured during head-sweeps to determine whether to begin a new run or initiate a second head-sweep.
source: In this work, we directly show that larvae do in fact use changes in odor receptor activity and light level measured during head-sweeps to determine whether to begin a new run or initiate a second head-sweep (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2E.

claim: For light and EtAc, larvae changed their rate of turning and the size of their turns in response to changing environmental conditions, but their speed of progress was the same whether conditions were improving or declining when engaged in forward movement.
source: For light and EtAc, larvae changed their rate of turning and the size of their turns in response to changing environmental conditions, but when they were actually engaged in forward movement, their speed of progress was the same whether conditions were improving or declining.
evidence: This is stated based on previous work by the authors.

claim: Larvae dramatically decreased their forward run speed in response to increases in the concentration of CO2.
source: In contrast, larvae dramatically decreased their forward run speed in response to increases in the concentration of CO2.
evidence: This is stated based on previous work by the authors.

claim: Larvae with non-functional CO2 receptors did not change their speed at all in response to CO2.
source: Larvae with non-functional CO2 receptors did not change their speed at all in response to CO2, so this modulation was due to a sensory-motor transformation and not to metabolic effects.
evidence: This is stated based on previous work by the authors.

claim: Larvae move forward through a series of tail to head peristaltic waves of muscle contraction.
source: Larvae move forward through a series of tail to head peristaltic waves of muscle contraction (Lahiri et al., 2011; Heckscher et al., 2012) and modulate their forward speed by changing the frequency with which they initiate these waves (Heckscher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Larvae modulate their forward speed by changing the frequency with which they initiate peristaltic waves.
source: Larvae move forward through a series of tail to head peristaltic waves of muscle contraction (Lahiri et al., 2011; Heckscher et al., 2012) and modulate their forward speed by changing the frequency with which they initiate these waves (Heckscher et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: To accept a head-sweep, larvae must initiate a new peristaltic wave.
source: In order to accept a head-sweep, that is, transition from head-sweeping to forward movement, larvae must initiate a new peristaltic wave (Lahiri et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation.

claim: If an increase in Gr21a activity decreases the probability of initiating a peristaltic wave, this would explain why an increase in Gr21a activity prior to head-sweep initiation results in an increased probability of head-sweep rejection.
source: If an increase in Gr21a activity decreases the probability of initiating such a wave, this would explain why an increase in Gr21a activity prior to head-sweep initiation results in an increased probability of head-sweep rejection (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observation in Figure 2E.

claim: An increase in Gr21a activity might bias the larva towards larger reorientations by decreasing the probability of quick, small course corrections.
source: Similarly, an increase in Gr21a activity might bias the larva towards larger reorientations (Figure 2D) by decreasing the probability of quick, small course corrections.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observation in Figure 2D.

claim: The maximum red light intensity (911 μW/cm2) was 300 times greater than the maximum blue light intensity (3 μW/cm2) in multi-sensory experiments.
source: For multi-sensory experiments, the maximum red light intensity (911 μW/cm2) was 300 times greater than the maximum blue light intensity (3 μW/cm2).
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: CsChrimson is slightly more sensitive to 655 nm than 448 nm light.
source: CsChrimson is slightly more sensitive to 655 nm than 448 nm light, so the blue light signal perturbed olfactory receptor neuron activity by less than 0.3% of the red-light signal's perturbation.
evidence: This is stated in the Materials and methods section.

claim: The blue light signal perturbed olfactory receptor neuron activity by less than 0.3% of the red-light signal's perturbation.
